title: Rose of Lima (1586–1617)
hookLine: a young woman in a garden hut in Lima, remembered as the first canonized saint of the Americas

lines: THE SICK IN HER PARENTS' HOUSE.
cards: At the back of a family garden in Lima, in Peru, stands a hut with barely room for one person. Inside, a young woman sews. Her needlework and the flowers she grows help keep her family fed.

Some days the door opens onto a different job: sick and hungry people from the city, whom she brings into a room of her parents' house and nurses herself. She never enters a convent. She never travels.
Yet the Church remembers her as the first person from the Americas to be named a saint. Her baptismal name was Isabel. In time she was called Rose.

teach.h: A ROSE, NAMED BY A SERVANT.
teach.b: Tradition says the name came from a servant who saw her as a baby and thought her face looked like a rose. She kept it. First, a life at home.
Rose wanted a life given to God, but she didn't join an enclosed convent.

teach.h: A TERTIARY IN A GARDEN HUT.
teach.b: She became a Dominican tertiary: a laywoman who follows the spirituality of the Dominicans while living in the world. Her cloister was a hut in the family garden. Second, the work of her hands.
She sewed and sold flowers to help her family, and took the poor and sick into her parents' house to nurse them herself.
Third, the hard part, told honestly. Rose practiced severe penances: fasting, sleeping on hard boards, wearing things meant to hurt. Her biographers called these heroic.
Some Catholics today read them more carefully, as signs of a fierce love that shouldn't be copied, and the Church doesn't ask anyone to imitate them. Fourth, the cross at the center.
Her spirituality kept returning to the suffering Christ.

Paul put it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." She belonged to a city of new wealth and old wounds, of conquerors and the conquered.
When the Church named her a saint, the Americas had their first. Lima still keeps her feast as its own.

how: Catholics in Peru and across Latin America keep the feast of Saint Rose of Lima, often with processions, and some Dominican laypeople look to her as a model of holiness lived outside a convent.

games.q: you're Rose. you want a life given to God, but you don't enter a convent. where do you live it?
o: in a convent in another city.
in a small hut in your family's garden.
games.why: she lived as a Dominican tertiary in a tiny garden hut, working for her family and caring for the sick.

practice: Picture a map from Mexico down to the far south, and let one place rise: a city you've heard of, a country in the news, a family you know from there.
If you pray, ask Rose of Lima to pray for it, or say a Hail Mary for its people; if not, simply hold them, the sick and the poor especially, the ones Rose brought into her parents' house.

wordCard.voice: Dominican tertiary. A laywoman who follows the spirituality of the Dominicans while living in the world, the life Rose of Lima chose instead of an enclosed convent.

carryVoice: Your line: first of the americas. A garden hut in Lima was room enough for a saint. See you tomorrow.
